The Story of Two Brothers and the Gems

I bow to the supreme Lord Jinendra, whose renunciation knows no limit beyond renunciation itself, and I write the story of two brothers who learned to fear worldly possessions.

In the land of Dasharn stood a beautiful city named Ekrath. There lived a merchant named Dhandatt, whose wife was Dhandatta. They had two sons, Dhandev and Dhanmitra, and a beautiful daughter named Dhanmitra.

After Dhandatt's death, through the ripening of sinful karma, the two brothers lost all their wealth and became utterly destitute. Hoping for some help, they went to their maternal uncle in Kaushambi and told him of their father's death with great sorrow. The uncle was deeply moved by their condition. He comforted them with many kind words and gave them eight precious gems so that they could rebuild their lives. Truly, this is what kinship means — to fulfil the hopes of those who come seeking help.

The two brothers took the gems and set out for home. But along the way, greed corrupted their hearts. Each began to desire the gems for himself alone, and murderous thoughts arose in both their minds. As they neared a village, good sense returned. Both deeply repented of their vile thoughts and confessed to each other, clearing the darkness from their hearts. They recognised the gems as the root cause of these sinful impulses, and so they cast them into the Vetravati River and went home.

A fish swallowed the gems, mistaking them for food. That same fish was caught in a fisherman's net. The fisherman killed it, found the gems inside, and sold them in the market. By the workings of karma, those very gems came into the hands of the two brothers' mother. Driven by greed, she plotted to kill her own children for the gems. But good sense arose in time, and she repented deeply, giving the gems to her daughter instead. Dhanmitra too was seized by greed and nearly committed a terrible act — until she too recovered her reason and cast the gems away once more.

Thus the gems passed from hand to hand, each time stirring murderous thoughts in those who possessed them. The brothers finally understood that worldly possessions are the root of violence and suffering. They renounced all desire for wealth, became monks, and through dedicated spiritual practice, attained liberation.

This story teaches the terrible danger of attachment to possessions. Wealth that should sustain life instead breeds greed, violence, and the destruction of the most sacred bonds — between brothers, between mother and child, between sister and brother. The wise recognise that true wealth is not gold and gems but the purity of the soul, and they renounce the possessions that bind them to suffering.
